title: Why We Need New Benchmarks for Local Intrinsic Dimension Estimation
claim: Samples from the proposed synthetic dataset are visually realistic yet lie on a manifold with controlled, known intrinsic dimension.
layout: 1 row of 6 grayscale image samples, left-to-right, thin white dividers
description: A single horizontal strip of six grayscale image samples separated by thin white vertical dividers. Each sample is a blurry, low-resolution side view of a sneaker or shoe, facing left with the toe on the left and the ankle opening on the right. The samples differ mainly in background brightness (dark gray to near black) and in the sheen and contrast of the shoe, plus small variations in shape. The blur suggests they are generated or decoded samples rather than crisp photos. There are no arrows, labels, annotations, or color. The eye goes first to the bright white shoe body against the dark backgrounds, then scans left to right to compare the small variations between samples.
caption: Few samples from Gaussian (IDR) dataset.
abstract: Neural Local Intrinsic Dimension (LID) estimators are typically bound to domain-specific architectures whose inductive biases can yield inconsistent estimates for the same underlying manifold. Existing evaluations either use overly simple synthetic data (with known LID) or real datasets (with unknown LID), obscuring true performance. We introduce a principled benchmarking framework that (i) maps the same manifold into multiple domain representations while preserving its structure, enabling like-for-like cross-architecture tests; (ii) designs harder variants of popular datasets that target key manifold properties; and (iii) applies controlled transformations with known LID shifts to stress-test methods even when absolute LID is unknown. Across this suite, including non-trivial synthetic datasets, we show that accuracy on simple manifolds does not transfer across domains and that state-of-the-art methods fail under targeted stressors, revealing clear failure modes and areas for improvement. Data and code are available: https://github.com/DominikFilipiak/LID-Benchmarks.
